kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-01.title: Factor 18
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-01.body:
The board has the numbers 2, 3, 5 and 7, all primes. The score is a product of these numbers, so we need the prime factorization $18 = 2\cdot 3\cdot 3$. It uses three factors, so Ali threw 3 darts (hitting 2, 3 and 3).

**Answer: (D) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-02.title: Compare sizes
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-02.body:
$12345$ is clearly the largest and $1 + 2345$ the second largest (both thousands). Among the three-digit sums, $123 + 45 = 168$ is smaller than $12 + 345 = 357$, so these are the two smallest, and $1234 + 5$ is in the middle.

**Answer: (D) $1234+5$**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-03.title: Read from the inside out
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-03.body:
Anne's mom's mom is Anne's grandma. A daughter of Anne's grandma is Anne's mom (or an aunt). The mother of that daughter is again Anne's grandma.

**Answer: (E) Anne's grandma**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-04.title: Follow a stripe
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-04.body:
Each stripe runs from the left front edge around the back to the right front edge. Worn properly, both ends of a stripe meet and it closes into a ring. In the right picture the two front halves are shifted by one stripe, so the end of each stripe meets the beginning of the next one. Following a stripe, you go around and continue on the next stripe, and so on: all stripes join into one long spiral with two free ends. There are **no** closed rings.

**Answer: (A) 0**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-05.title: Add the digits by place
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-05.body:
On the left, $\overline{AB} + \overline{CD} = 10A + B + 10C + D = 79$. On the right,

$$\overline{AD} + \overline{CD} + \overline{AB} + \overline{CB} = 20A + 20C + 2B + 2D = 2(10A + B + 10C + D) = 2\cdot 79 = 158.$$

**Answer: (B) 158**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-05.title: Tens and units
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-05.body:
The right column uses each of A and C twice as a tens digit and each of B and D twice as a units digit — exactly the digits of the left sum, each used twice. So the total is $2\cdot79 = 158$.

**Answer: (B) 158**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-06.title: Equation
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-06.body:
If the least is $n$, then $n + (n+1) + (n+2) + (n+3) = 4n + 6 = 2$, so $n = -1$. The integers are $-1, 0, 1, 2$.

**Answer: (C) $-1$**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-06.title: Guess and check
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-06.body:
$-1 + 0 + 1 + 2 = 2$ ✓. Starting at $-2$ gives $-2$, starting at $0$ gives $6$.

**Answer: (C) $-1$**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-07.title: Next repeated block
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-07.body:
Such years are $\overline{abab} = 101\cdot\overline{ab}$. After $2020 = 101\cdot 20$ the next one is $101\cdot 21 = 2121$, which is $101$ years later.

**Answer: (B) 101**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-08.title: Count vertices
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-08.body:
The three cut squares became 6 triangles with $18$ vertices. The other 7 pieces have $42 - 18 = 24$ vertices. If $s$ of them are squares and $t$ triangles: $s + t = 7$ and $4s + 3t = 24$. Subtracting $3(s + t) = 21$ gives $s = 3$, so $t = 4$ triangles.

**Answer: (E) 4**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-08.title: Start with all triangles
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-08.body:
If the 7 uncut pieces were all triangles, they would have 21 vertices; each square adds one more. We need $24$, so 3 are squares and $7 - 3 = 4$ are triangles.

**Answer: (E) 4**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-09.title: Midsegments
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-09.body:
A segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is half as long as the third side. Each of the four connecting pieces joins the midpoints of two neighbouring sides of the kite, so it is half of a diagonal: two of them are $60$ cm and two are $40$ cm. The pole was $120 + 80 + 2\cdot 60 + 2\cdot 40 = 400$ cm long.

**Answer: (C) 400 cm**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-10.title: Check the four triangles
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-10.body:
With the bottom-left corner as origin, the points are $P = (1,4)$, $Q = (2,4)$, $R = (5,3)$, $S = (2,1)$.

- $PQR$: base $PQ = 1$ (horizontal), height $4 - 3 = 1$: area $\frac12$.
- $PQS$: base 1, height 3: $\frac32$.
- $QRS$: base $QS = 3$ (vertical), height 3: $\frac92$.
- $PRS$: the largest, $\frac{11}{2}$.

The smallest area is $\frac12$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac12$**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-11.title: Two weeks plus four days
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-11.body:
18 days are two full weeks (6 story days, whatever the start) plus 4 more days, which have the same weekdays as the first 4 days of the visit. So we want 4 consecutive days containing as many of Tuesday, Saturday, Sunday as possible. Saturday–Sunday–Monday–Tuesday contains all three; any other start gives at most 2. So she should start on **Saturday** (9 story days).

**Answer: (D) Saturday**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-12.title: Twice a square
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-12.body:
$abcd = (ab)(cd) = 2cd\cdot cd = 2(cd)^2$, so $abcd$ must be twice a perfect square. $50 = 2\cdot 25$, $200 = 2\cdot100$, $450 = 2\cdot 225$, $800 = 2\cdot 400$ work, but $100 = 2\cdot 50$ and 50 is not a square. So 100 is impossible.

**Answer: (B) 100**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-13.title: Put everything on a line
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-13.body:
The left signpost is 3 km from Atown and 9 km from Cetown, so the road from Atown to Cetown is 12 km long. Betown is 1 km beyond it, i.e. $3 + 1 = 4$ km from Atown. The right signpost is 6 km from Atown (and 6 km from Cetown ✓). It is $6 - 4 = 2$ km past Betown, so the broken sign said **2 km**.

**Answer: (B) 2 km**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-14.title: Two cases
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-14.body:
The other two sides are $x$ and $\frac25 x$, and two of the three sides are equal. They can't be equal to each other, so one of them is 20.

- $x = 20$: sides $20, 20, 8$ — a valid triangle, perimeter $48$ cm.
- $\frac25 x = 20$: $x = 50$, sides $20, 20, 50$ — impossible, as $20 + 20 < 50$.

So the perimeter is 48 cm.

**Answer: (B) 48 cm**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-15.title: Add the diameters
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-15.body:
The four diameters together contain each outer number once and the centre $c$ four times: $4\cdot 13 = 40 + 4c$. So $4c = 12$ and $c = 3$.

**Answer: (A) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-15.title: One diameter at a time
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-15.body:
Each diameter is the centre plus two opposite outer numbers. The four pairs of outer numbers add up to 40 together, so on average a pair adds up to 10, and since every pair has the same sum $13 - c$, $13 - c = 10$ and $c = 3$.

**Answer: (A) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-16.title: Simulate
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-16.body:
First round: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Remaining: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13. Going on from 12, she skips 13 and pops **1**, skips 3 and pops 5, skips 7 and pops 9, skips 11 and pops 13, then skips 3 and pops 7, skips 11 and pops 3, and finally 11.

The full order is $2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 1, 5, 9, 13, 7, 3, 11$. Of the given pairs, only 12 and 1 are popped one right after the other.

**Answer: (C) 12 and 1**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-17.title: Follow the directions of the lines
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-17.body:
Measure directions as angles from the base of the triangle. The left side of the triangle points up at $60^\circ$. The top side of the big square makes $70^\circ$ with it, so it points at $60^\circ - 70^\circ = -10^\circ$ (slightly downwards to the right). The right side of the big square is perpendicular to it, pointing up at $80^\circ$.

The small square has a side on the right side of the triangle, which points at $-60^\circ$; its top side is perpendicular to that, pointing at $30^\circ$.

The angle marked ? is between the big square's side (at $80^\circ$) and the small square's top side (at $30^\circ$): $80^\circ - 30^\circ = 50^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) 50°**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-17.title: Angle chasing in a triangle
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-17.body:
Extend the top side of the big square from its corner P on the left side of the triangle until it meets the right side at R. In triangle $TPR$ (T the top vertex) the angles are $60^\circ$ at T and $70^\circ$ at P, so $\angle TRP = 50^\circ$: the big square's top side makes $50^\circ$ with the triangle's right side. The big square's right side is perpendicular to its top side, and the small square's top side is perpendicular to the triangle's right side. Turning both lines by $90^\circ$ keeps the angle between them, so the marked angle is $50^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) 50°**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-18.title: Two conditions
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-18.body:
After 55 km, $14 - 5.5 = 8.5$ litres are left: enough for 85 km. So the station must be at most 85 km ahead (95 km is too far).

From the sign, $520 - 55 = 465$ km remain. A full tank lasts 400 km, so after filling up at most 400 km may remain: the station must be at least $465 - 400 = 65$ km ahead.

Only the station 75 km ahead satisfies both.

**Answer: (D) 75 km**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-19.title: Total in two ways
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-19.body:
The sum of all nine numbers equals the sum of the three rows: $24 + 26 + B$, and also the sum of the three columns: $27 + 20 + A$. So $50 + B = 47 + A$, i.e. $A - B = 3$.

**Answer: (B) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-20.title: Use the top triangle
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-20.body:
The window has side 9 dm, and each triangle has area $\frac{81}{6} = 13.5$ dm². The top triangle has the whole top side (9 dm) as its base and the fly's spot as its apex, so its height $h$ satisfies $\frac12\cdot 9\cdot h = 13.5$, i.e. $h = 3$ dm. The fly is 3 dm below the top, i.e. $9 - 3 = 6$ dm above the bottom.

**Answer: (D) 6 dm**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-21.title: Middle number
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-21.body:
With an odd number of consecutive integers, the middle one is the average: $\frac{2020}{101} = 20$. The smallest and largest are $20 - 50 = -30$ and $20 + 50 = 70$, with sum $40$.

**Answer: (B) 40**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-21.title: Pairing
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-21.body:
Pair the smallest with the largest, the second smallest with the second largest, etc. All pairs have the same sum $s$, and there are 50 pairs plus the middle number $\frac s2$. So $50s + \frac s2 = 2020$, i.e. $101\cdot\frac s2 = 2020$ and $s = 40$.

**Answer: (B) 40**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-22.title: Right triangle
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-22.body:
In the same time the hare runs 5 times as far as the tortoise: 25 km. If he ran $x$ km perpendicular to the route, the turning point is $\sqrt{5^2 + x^2}$ km from the finish and $x + \sqrt{25 + x^2} = 25$. So $25 + x^2 = (25 - x)^2 = 625 - 50x + x^2$, giving $x = 12$ and the distance $25 - 12 = 13$ km.

**Answer: (C) 13 km**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-22.title: Pythagorean triple
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-22.body:
We need a right triangle with one leg 5 and the other leg plus hypotenuse equal to 25. The triple $5, 12, 13$ fits: $12 + 13 = 25$. The distance from the turning point to the finish is the hypotenuse, 13 km.

**Answer: (C) 13 km**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-23.title: Chain the rules
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-23.body:
Take a blue figure. By rule 2 it is a triangle. By rule 1, a large figure would be a square, so a triangle cannot be large — it is small. Hence every blue figure is small: (E).

The others need not hold: a small red triangle breaks (A) and (D); a small red square breaks (B) and (C).

**Answer: (E) All blue figures are small.**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-24.title: The overlap is a rhombus
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-24.body:
The overlap is a parallelogram whose two pairs of sides lie on the long sides of the two rectangles; since both strips have the same width 3, all its sides are equal — it is a rhombus with side $s$. In the horizontal rectangle, the rhombus has one side of length $s$ along the bottom, and the part of the bottom side outside it has length $9 - s$. The slanted side of the rhombus is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 3 (height) and $9 - s$: $s^2 = 3^2 + (9 - s)^2$, so $18s = 90$ and $s = 5$. Area $= \text{base}\cdot\text{height} = 5\cdot 3 = 15$ cm².

**Answer: (D) 15 cm²**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-25.title: Pythagoras on the grid
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-25.body:
Let the grid squares have side $u$. From the picture, B is 3 squares right and 4 squares down from A, and C is 5 squares right and 2 squares down. So $AB = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2}\,u = 5u = 1$, i.e. $u = \frac15$, and $AC = \sqrt{5^2 + 2^2}\,u = \frac{\sqrt{29}}{5}$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{\sqrt{29}}{5}$**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-26.title: Two arrangements
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-26.body:
The cube is $4\times4\times4$; each face has 16 small faces. A small cube has two painted faces exactly when it lies on an edge shared by two painted faces, so we want painted faces sharing as few edges as possible. Three faces either meet at a corner or consist of two opposite faces and one between them.

- Three faces at a corner: they share 3 edges; each face loses its cells on 2 shared edges, keeping a $3\times3$ block: $3\cdot 9 = 27$.
- Two opposite faces plus a face between them: the middle face shares an edge with each, keeping $4\cdot 2 = 8$ cells; each opposite face shares one edge and keeps $16 - 4 = 12$. Total $8 + 12 + 12 = 32$.

The maximum is 32.

**Answer: (C) 32**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-27.title: Use the common sum S
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-27.body:
Let S be the common sum. The third column contains $6 + 2 + 7$ and one unknown, so that unknown is $S - 15$; the second row gives its first cell $S - 12$. In the third row, the unknown in the third column is $S - 15$, so its first cell is $S - 7 - 4 - (S - 15) = 4$. Then the first column gives the shaded cell: $S - 1 - (S - 12) - 4 = 7$, whatever S is.

**Answer: (C) 7**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-27.title: Check with a full square
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-27.body:
With $S = 16$: rows $1, 6, 6, 3$; $4, 2, 2, 8$; $4, 7, 1, 4$; $7, 1, 7, 1$ — every row and column sums to 16, and the shaded cell (first cell of the last row) is 7.

**Answer: (C) 7**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-28.title: Count the games
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-28.body:
Every game has two players, so there were $\frac{10 + 15 + 17}{2} = 21$ games. A girl who rests plays in the next game, so nobody rests twice in a row. Alice played 10 of the 21 games and rested in 11. Resting 11 times in 21 games without two rests in a row is only possible as games $1, 3, 5, \ldots, 21$. So Alice played games $2, 4, \ldots, 20$ and lost each of them (she rested right after). In particular, Alice lost the second game.

**Answer: (A) Alice**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-29.title: Equal arcs between the peaks
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-29.body:
Call the peaks $P_1, \ldots, P_4$ (on the semicircle).

- The angle $\angle P_1AB = \alpha$ is inscribed and subtends the arc $P_1B$, so arc $P_1B = 2\alpha$ and arc $AP_1 = 180^\circ - 2\alpha$. In the same way arc $P_4B = 180^\circ - 2\alpha$.
- Between two peaks $P_k$ and $P_{k+1}$ the line goes down to the diameter at Q and up again, both at angle $\alpha$. Extend $P_kQ$ beyond Q until it meets the circle at X. By symmetry in the diameter, X is the mirror image of $P_{k+1}$, so $XP_{k+1}$ is perpendicular to AB. Then the inscribed angle $\angle P_kXP_{k+1} = 90^\circ - \alpha$, so arc $P_kP_{k+1} = 180^\circ - 2\alpha$.

So the semicircle is split into 5 equal arcs of $180^\circ - 2\alpha$: $5(180^\circ - 2\alpha) = 180^\circ$, giving $\alpha = 72^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) 72°**

kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-30.title: Last digits and lcm
kangaroo-ca-2020-g0910-30.body:
None of them can end in 0 (no division by 0), so the eight last digits are $1, \ldots, 8$ or $2, \ldots, 9$. Write the numbers as $10k + d$. Then $d \mid 10k + d$ means $d \mid 10k$ for each of the eight digits.

- Digits $2, \ldots, 9$: $10k$ must be divisible by $\operatorname{lcm}(2, \ldots, 9) = 2520$, too big for a three-digit number.
- Digits $1, \ldots, 8$: $10k$ divisible by $\operatorname{lcm}(1, \ldots, 8) = 840$, so $10k = 840$: the numbers $841, \ldots, 848$.

The smallest is 841 with digit sum $8 + 4 + 1 = 13$.

**Answer: (D) 13**
